posts.note: Satire-framed post on Billy Evans's pet blood-testing startup Haemanthus. Two third-party company plans logged with own_claim false; two RAMHT event announcements logged as CONTROL candidates.
Event-day post on GrayMatters Health PRISM neurofeedback. Contains an internal inconsistency on whether an FDA depression clearance was obtained or is still pending.
Argument that GAD is not a valid diagnosis; the proposed criterion rewrite is normative with no predictive reading. No forward-looking statements.
Retrospective analysis of Shields et al. (JAMA Psychiatry 2025) on PE-owned psychiatric hospitals. One borderline item about the author's own litigation logged.
Transcript of a 2020 podcast republished 2025-05-26. Two generalized claims about police behavior logged as borderline. Third-party speakers' statements are not adopted and not logged.
130-word podcast blurb; 'we should consider making it less miserable' is normative. Nothing logged.
Republished book chapter on fluoxetine history. One own-content promise logged. 'Neuromodulation as a first-line treatment' is a present practice stance, not logged.
Memoir of the author's first Zoloft dose in 1995 and a manic episode; no forward-looking statements.
Announcement of the author's co-authored TD AI detection paper (J Clin Psychiatry 2025) and the free TDscreen.ai tool. Three AI/screening forecasts and one Radial expansion claim logged.

statements.quote: Brief promotional note: I have an in-person, live, exciting, and other adjectives, newsletter event in Los Angeles on May 18, with a thrilling speaker lineup.
statements.context: Promotional aside near the top of a satire post about Billy Evans (Elizabeth Holmes's husband) and his pet blood-testing startup Haemanthus. The author announces his own live newsletter event, Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment (RAMHT), in Los Angeles on May 18, 2025, two days after the post.
statements.note: Own-event announcement; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: We're going to be announcing brand new treatments for depression, for heaven's sake.
statements.context: Same promotional aside: the author says the RAMHT Los Angeles event on May 18, 2025 will announce brand new treatments for depression.
statements.note: Own-event content promise; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: as much as I actually believe that the total addressable market of a disruptive company in the lab testing space could possibly be huge
statements.context: The author revisits his earlier satirical article arguing that Theranos's investment thesis is still venture-fundable. He states sincerely that the total addressable market for a disruptive lab-testing company could be huge, before saying he meant the article as satire because Elizabeth Holmes is in jail for fraud.
statements.note: Hedged market-potential claim; weakly forward-looking.

statements.quote: It's her husband, who's not in jail. At least, not yet.
statements.context: The author notes that Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes's husband, is raising money for Haemanthus, a pet blood-testing startup that uses lasers in a small box like the Theranos Edison. 'At least, not yet' insinuates that Evans may end up in jail too.
statements.note: Quip/insinuation in a satire-framed post; the author appears to sincerely doubt the venture's legitimacy. Borderline.

statements.quote: It plans to begin with testing pets for diseases before progressing to humans
statements.context: Block quote from The New York Times reproduced by the author about Haemanthus, Billy Evans's blood-testing startup: it plans to start with pet disease testing and later move to humans, with marketing materials that hope to raise more than $50 million toward 'human health optimization'.
statements.note: Third-party company plan quoted from the NYT; the author mocks it rather than adopting it.

statements.quote: the marketing materials say the Haemanthus’ long-term goals include developing a small, wearable version of the device for humans
statements.context: Block quote from The Guardian (referencing the NYT) reproduced by the author: Haemanthus's marketing materials say its long-term goals include a small wearable version of its laser blood/saliva/urine testing device for humans.
statements.note: Third-party company goal quoted from press; not adopted by the author.

statements.quote: Not just blood, but spit too! Not just the too-small-for-realistic-physics MiniLab, but a wearable device! Get out your checkbooks, investors. This will go big or go home.
statements.context: The author's sarcastic reaction to Haemanthus's marketing claims (laser scan of blood, saliva or urine from pets in seconds; a wearable device for humans). He calls the device 'too-small-for-realistic-physics', echoing Theranos's MiniLab, and says the venture will 'go big or go home'. The implied claim is that the technology is physically implausible and the venture is a boom-or-bust bet he expects to fail.
statements.note: Sarcastic framing; the sincere underlying claim is that the device is physically implausible. Compound.

statements.quote: implausible testing that raises millions at the expense of vulnerable people and, now, pets
statements.context: Closing line of the Haemanthus section: the author says the Holmes/Evans family 'carries the flame' for implausible testing that raises millions at the expense of vulnerable people and, now, pets. Implicit claim that Haemanthus's testing will not work as promised.
statements.note: Borderline: characterization with an implicit forecast that the technology will not deliver.

statements.quote: Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment LA 2025 is Tonight! This is an event at which experts will have rapid conversations about rapid-acting treatments.
statements.context: Opening of a post published on the day of the author's live RAMHT LA 2025 event (2025-05-18, 6 pm, Los Angeles), co-created with Grady Hannah. Announces the event and its format.
statements.note: Own-event announcement; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: we have to gather more data before it gets clearance for the indication of depression treatment
statements.context: About GrayMatters Health's PRISM EEG-fMRI-pattern neurofeedback (PRISM Suite). The author says an alternate algorithm for depression has been studied in a small sample (49 people) and evaluated as safe by the FDA, and that more data must be gathered before it gets FDA clearance for the depression indication. Earlier in the same post he writes 'They just got another FDA clearance, this time for use in depression'.
statements.note: Presupposes eventual FDA clearance of PRISM for depression; conflicts with the earlier line saying a depression clearance was just obtained.

statements.quote: which I will dig into more soon when I don’t have set up for my event this evening
statements.context: The author promises to analyze PRISM's MDD (depression) data in more depth soon, after the RAMHT event that evening.
statements.note: Own-content promise; CONTROL candidate; low forecast value.

statements.quote: The first is that it may prove another practical option for treating depression without medicine or external stimulation of any kind.
statements.context: First of two reasons the author finds PRISM's MDD data exciting: PRISM neurofeedback (the brain as its own stimulator, no medication or external stimulation) may become another practical depression treatment option.
statements.note: Hedged. The author uses PRISM at Fermata and GrayMatters Health sponsors his event.

statements.quote: The future of mental health is effective . It's not just medicines and therapy. It's changing your brain in ways it’s hard to imagine —safely, quickly, and for the better.
statements.context: Closing thesis after discussing PRISM's ML-trained EEG neurofeedback for PTSD and depression: the author asserts that the future of mental health treatment is effective brain-changing treatments, not just medicines and therapy.
statements.note: Broad, undated field-level forecast.

statements.quote: Yes, that would be a grievance I am leaving to the courts to settle.
statements.context: Aside in a post analyzing a JAMA Psychiatry paper (Shields et al., 2025) on private equity-owned freestanding psychiatric hospitals. The author acknowledges active litigation with Amanda Itzkoff, M.D. and Jack Wolcowitz, who acquired his prior practice, and says the courts will settle the grievance.
statements.note: Borderline: implies a future court resolution of the author's own litigation; low forecast value.

statements.quote: You're going to pull that trigger. More often than not. And that's about a thousand times a year.
statements.context: Podcast transcript recorded in 2020 after George Floyd's killing, republished 2025-05-26. The author argues that an armed police officer called to a mental-health crisis, told to protect himself and knowing no consequences follow, will shoot 'more often than not', about a thousand times a year.
statements.note: Generalized behavioral claim from a 2020 recording; not a dated forecast. Borderline.

statements.quote: Nothing's going to stop them if they want to. And they do. On camera. A thousand other times every year.
statements.context: Same 2020 recording: the author says Black Americans know police can kill them and that nothing will stop police from doing so, about a thousand times every year.
statements.note: Generalized claim from a 2020 recording republished in 2025; borderline forward-looking. Footnote 2 (2025) adds that a few officers have since been found guilty.

statements.quote: I'm editing an FDA-approval trial publication day, so you're gonna have to wait until I'm done with that for fresh new content
statements.context: Intro to a republished essay on Prozac, the first chapter of the author's book Inessential Pharmacology. The author says he is editing an FDA-approval trial publication and that fresh new content will follow when he is done.
statements.note: Own-content promise; CONTROL candidate. Also signals the author is working on an FDA-approval trial publication.

statements.quote: As we ponder which jobs AI will displace, I have initiated the trend by displacing myself
statements.context: Post announcing publication of the author's co-authored J Clin Psychiatry paper on video-based AI detection of tardive dyskinesia (TD), ROC-AUC 0.89, n=351. The author says AI will displace jobs and that he, a human rater in the trial, was outperformed by the algorithm.
statements.note: Presupposition that AI will displace jobs, including TD rating; borderline.

statements.quote: Screening millions of people for a potentially debilitating adverse effect, however, is something we can feel good about automating away
statements.context: Same post: the author frames AI-based TD screening as a task that will be automated, screening millions of people for tardive dyskinesia, a potentially debilitating medication adverse effect.
statements.note: Implicit forecast that TD screening will be automated at scale; borderline.

statements.quote: It provides hope that more and more screening tasks can be accomplished more effectively, faster, and more frequently, allowing clinicians to focus on diagnosis and treatment.
statements.context: Same post: from a small two-site sample (n=351) in which the model beat human raters, the author extrapolates that more and more screening tasks will be done by AI more effectively, faster and more frequently, freeing clinicians for diagnosis and treatment.
statements.note: Hedged field-level forecast.

statements.quote: We aren’t available in every state yet, but we are working on it!
statements.context: Closing call to action to schedule with a doctor on the author's team at Radial. Radial is not yet available in every US state but is working on expansion.
statements.note: Own-company expansion claim; CONTROL candidate.
